zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida; CC BY 4.0. Supplied index: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The transcription and explanatory notes are this reviewer's scan-based work; the index is an identification aid, not diplomatic authority.

lines.note: The continuation means serving until the end of one's life; the Portuguese explicitly says to serve until death. The preceding portion of the Japanese example belongs to the previous page.
Ino ko is explained as inoshishi no ko, a young wild boar. The Portuguese begins 'a piglet, offspring of'; the damaged, closely set letters in filho replace the OCR's fuho.
Porco montes completes the identification as a wild-boar piglet, rather than a domestic pig. The short continuation is a complete physical row.

runs.text: Ino cogumo. i, Inocono gotocu madarana cu

lines.note: Ino kogumo is explained by clouds mottled like a young boar. The Japanese explanation continues with cu plus mouo on the next row; no line-end hyphen is supplied where none is visible.

Completes kumo wo yuu, 'clouds so called'; the Portuguese describes clouds appearing laden. The narrow internal division in car rega- is retained provisionally rather than silently regularized to modern carregadas.

runs.text: das & de varias cores, asquaes ſaõ ſinal de grã

lines.note: Das completes the preceding Portuguese participle. The clouds have various colours and are said to indicate a great wind or storm; the printed abbreviation grã continues into de on the next row.
Completes grande vento, with tempestade offering the alternative 'storm'. This closes the weather explanation for the cloud name.

runs.text: Horas cõforme à conta de Iapaõ deſ-

lines.note: Ino koku is the boar-hour in the Japanese reckoning described by the dictionary. The gloss's deſ- continues with das below; the actual numerical interval follows on the next line.
The dictionary gives the interval as ten at night to twelve. The final number is visibly 12, not the OCR's Iz; the source's time convention is retained without modern adjustment.

runs.text: Naõ atirar com todas as ſe

lines.note: Inokoshi, inokosu, inokoshita describes leaving some arrows unshot. The Portuguese says not to shoot with all the arrows; atirar replaces OCR atirur, and ſe continues into tas without a printed hyphen.
Tas completes setas, 'arrows', and therefore the negative definition of leaving arrows unused. It is not a separate entry.
Inokozuchi names a herb. The gloss only says 'a herb so called', so no botanical identification is added to the transcription.
Inomoto is glossed as a water well. The contracted historical spelling dagua is preserved, not expanded into modern d'água or de água.
Inoke means driving something away by shooting arrows. The Portuguese verb is Afaſtar, with a t in the joined st group, rather than the OCR's Afaſſar.
Inoki is the tusk or tooth of a wild boar. Preſa here means a tusk, as the following explanation makes clear, not prey or a captive.
Inori denotes prayers or supplications; gentilicas classifies them as non-Christian in the compilers' terminology. The note explains the historical gloss without adopting its religious evaluation.
The verb inoru is glossed as making supplications. Its principal parts include otta; the divided Fo- begins the following example addressed to a Buddha.
Completes Fotoqeni, with Fotoqeuo inoru as the alternative construction: praying to or invoking a Buddha. The Latin l introduces the alternative and is not part of the Japanese wording.

Inorikoroshi means killing by imprecation or ritual prayer. The faint type between o and ta supports oita, the historical principal-part ending, rather than leaving the OCR gap o ta; the gloss continues below. The supplied NINJAL entry 132a11 independently supports the identification; the i remains weak in this impression.
Completes deprecações and adds 'or spells'. Together these describe the means of killing in the preceding headword, not an ordinary physical attack.
Inorinoke is illustrated by expelling a tengu through prayer. The headword and divided example mutually clarify the weak middle letters; Vt is the italic example marker.

runs.text: Botar fora com deprecações ao de

lines.note: Rinoquru completes inorinoquru, to drive away through prayer; the weak n is read in conjunction with the repeated headword. The Portuguese begins expelling the demon by supplications, with demonio divided after de. The damaged right shoulder of n remains a nonblocking reading uncertainty.
Monio completes demonio, the Portuguese designation used here for the tengu. This short line closes the exorcism example.
Inoritsuke is the contrasting operation: causing a spirit to enter someone through spells and supplications. The Portuguese explanation continues on the next two rows.

runs.text: deprecações entrar em alguem o demonio, ra-

lines.note: The objects made to enter a person are the demon and a fox; ra- continues into raposa. This is the dictionary's account of spirit possession, not a new example of expulsion.
Poſa completes raposa, 'fox', and the list of spirits or agents of possession. The continuation belongs to inoritsuke.
Inpon is equated with surihon, a printed book. The initial I is not preceded by another l; the final upright S is the dictionary's written-usage label.

Inket is explained by a phrase involving moist blood and glossed as human seed or semen. The final t belongs to the historical Sino-Japanese spelling and is not expanded; the visible circumflex in Vruuô is retained.
Inki first denotes stuffiness or oppression. Inqi xita, not the OCR's Iuqi xita, begins an example of a confined, airless place; the noun tocoro is divided at the line end.
Ro completes tocoro; the Portuguese says 'a cramped and stuffy place'. Itẽ introduces a second, emotional sense of the same word.

runs.text: Inqi xita. l, qiga inqi xita.

lines.note: The paired examples describe feeling oppressed or heavy in spirit. The Portuguese begins 'I have my heart'; co- continues into coração below.
Completes coração apertado e abafado, a constricted or oppressed heart. This is the emotional counterpart to the airless-place example above.

runs.text: Certa laya de peça com lauores douro.

lines.note: This is a gold-ornamented fabric. The final printed type has a u-shaped bottom and is retained as Inqiu; the next entry clearly reads Inqin. The subsequently consulted NINJAL index (132a17) identifies this entry too as Inqin, but the possible damaged or inverted n is not silently substituted for the local u-shaped impression.

runs.text: Certa peça de ſeda dourada da China.

lines.note: Inqin is specified as a gold-decorated silk fabric from China. The scan has initial capital I and capital C in China, unlike the draft's lowercase forms.
The adjectival form inqina applies either to an airless place or to an oppressed heart. It resumes the two senses of Inqi, not the intervening gold-fabric entries.
'E apertado' completes the characterization as confined or constricted. Both the physical place and the figurative heart remain possible referents.
Inqini is the corresponding adverb, explicitly labelled Adu. Its indentation is visible and retained; the lack of a separate Portuguese paraphrase does not make this a missing line.
Inkyo is explained by withdrawing from public life. The Portuguese starts with handing the inheritance to a son; herança has h, not OCR b, and the recipient continues below.

runs.text: filho, ou renunciar o eſtado, ou renda, &c.

lines.note: Completes the transfer to the son, or renunciation of one's position or income. The clearly comparable filho also helps resolve the closely printed letters in line c1-l002.

runs.text: & recolherſe como fazem em Iapão. Vt,

lines.note: The gloss continues with retiring or secluding oneself, described as a Japanese practice. In- starts the example inqio suru; the local tilde in Iapão remains on a.
Completes inqio suru, 'to retire', with Idem referring back to the preceding explanation. The example remains divided according to the printed lineation.
Inraku denotes sensual pleasure, evaluated negatively by the Portuguese gloss. The opening reads Inracu, not OCR ſuracu, and carnaes has the expected r-n sequence rather than cornaes.
Inran is paraphrased in Japanese as disorderly indulgence and glossed as sensuality. This separate headword supplies the basis for the prohibition in the next line.
The example prohibits making sensual indulgence one's occupation. The visible tilde in Inrãuo abbreviates the final nasal before uo; the Portuguese negative Não governs the following line.

runs.text: vos deis aos goſtos da carne.

lines.note: Completes 'do not give yourselves over to the pleasures of the flesh'. This translates the preceding negative injunction rather than introducing another sense.

runs.text: Bocetinhas onde metem mezinhas, ou ou-

lines.note: Inro are small cases used to hold medicines or other things. The headword begins with a capital I, and the circumflex over o is visible; ou- starts outras on the next row.

runs.text: tras couſas, que tem huns repartimentos encaxa-

lines.note: Completes outras couſas and describes nested compartments in the cases. The ending of tras is s, not OCR r; encaxa- continues into dos below.
Completes encaxados hum no outro, compartments fitted one into another. This is the last body row of the column, not a catchword.

Insoku is paraphrased by an obstruction or overshadowing and defined as the roads being blocked. The scan preserves n after the initial I; Eſtarẽ carries an abbreviation tilde, not the draft's grave accent.
Tapados completes the statement that the roads are closed or blocked. This continuation supplies the predicate of the preceding Portuguese phrase.
Insu denotes fine gold, explicitly equated with twenty-four-carat gold in the gloss. The number belongs to the definition, not a source reference.
Insui is explained as nomu mizu, water one drinks. The Portuguese repeats the drinking-water meaning directly.
This separate homographic Insui means human seed or semen. It is not a continuation of the preceding drinking-water definition.
Intoku is explained as hidden virtue. The Portuguese pairs virtues with merits, with mere- continuing into merecimentos below.
Completes 'hidden merits'. The terminal upright S marks written usage and is not part of the italic gloss.
Inton means retreat from worldly life; the Japanese paraphrase is kakure nogaruru. The extra i in the draft's nogaruiru is unsupported by the row; mun- begins mundo below.

runs.text: do, ou retirarſe do mundo como quem faz

lines.note: Completes mundo and describes withdrawing from the world, as someone who practices the retirement named on the next row. The Japanese cross-reference is part of this Portuguese sentence.

Inquio is the embedded Japanese name for retirement, referring to the Inqio entry in the other column. Its visible italic type and the extra u in this occurrence are retained, rather than conformed to that headword.
Inu means dog; inu ga hoyuru is the example 'the dog barks'. The Portuguese equivalent is divided before its subject on the following row.
After completing 'the dog barks', the entry introduces inu no koku, the dog-hour. Oi- starts the numerical interval oito, 'eight'.

runs.text: to da noite tè as dez. ¶ Item, Esta pala-

lines.note: The dictionary gives the dog-hour as eight to ten at night. It then begins a grammatical explanation of the word inu, with palavra divided at the line end.
Completes palavra and explicitly discusses Inu compounded with names of trees. Inu is a Japanese term embedded in a Portuguese explanation, unlike the headword or standalone examples above.

runs.text: fruitas, &c. às vezes ſignifica não ſer a-

lines.note: The explanation extends to fruits and says the compound can indicate that the named thing is not the genuine article. A- continues into aquella below.

runs.text: quella aruore, ou fruita propria, & boa como

lines.note: Completes the comparison with the proper or good tree or fruit. This is the dictionary's account of the depreciatory or wild-variety use of inu in compounds.

runs.text: ſe vera a baixo nalgũs exemplos.

lines.note: The reader is directed to examples below. The historical separated a baixo and abbreviated nalgũs remain as printed.

runs.text: Boceta com que folgão os mininos fei

lines.note: Inubako is a small box with which children play. The description of its manufacture starts with fei, completed as feita on the next row without adding a hyphen.

runs.text: ta de pasta de papel à maneira, & figura

lines.note: The box is made of paper pulp in a particular form. Pasta de papel explains the material; the animal shape is supplied in the next short row.
The box is shaped like a dog. This completes the description of inubako rather than introducing a second dog entry.
Inubai names a fly associated with dogs. The gloss does not provide enough detail to assign a modern biological species.

runs.text: Certo caminho muito estreito por on-

lines.note: Inubashiri denotes a very narrow passage. The divided onde introduces the description of movement along a fortification on the next row.

runs.text: de paßão eſcaſamente ao longo da fortaleza.

lines.note: Completes the explanation: a passage along the fortress where one can scarcely pass. Ao longo replaces the garbled OCR anlongo. Reinspection against aßi and Treſpaßar confirms the double-s ligature in paßão, rather than a single long s or two separately transcribed long-s types.
Inugiri is defined relative to the tree qiri. The small final a in Hũa is weak but present; Qiri is an upright Japanese tree name embedded in the otherwise Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: he tão boa, ou he mais ſilueſtre.

lines.note: The tree is said to be less good or more wild than ordinary qiri. This exemplifies the compound use of inu explained above.
Inui is the northwestern direction, explained as between west and north. The small separator between u and i is retained as a hyphen; the Portuguese Northwest word is divided after No.
Completes Noroeste and gives the example inui no hoo, 'the northwestern direction'. The scan supports Inu-i, not OCR Inua i; the long-o mark in fǒ is a caron.

runs.text: O morrer fora de tempo, ou lugar ſem

lines.note: Inujini is an ill-timed or misplaced death, with the following row specifying the lack of a notable military deed. The Portuguese explanation should be read through the line break.

runs.text: fazer couſa inſigne na guerra. Vt,

lines.note: The death occurs without doing anything distinguished in war. Inujini begins the example completed by the verbal construction on the next row.
The object particle and suru complete inujini wo suru, to die a futile death. This is part of the Japanese example, not Portuguese prose.

runs.text: Ponta da bainha de cima que ſe

lines.note: Inumaneki denotes the projecting end of an outer scabbard or protective covering. The Portuguese identifies it by its position and continues with its protective function.

runs.text: poem por reſguardo da propria, aqual ſobeja,

lines.note: The outer covering protects the actual scabbard and projects beyond it. Poem is retained without adding a modern accent; aqual is printed as one word here.
The end extends a little beyond the protected scabbard. This closes the definition of the projecting protective tip.

runs.text: Das oito horas tè as dez da noite.

lines.note: Inu no koku is separately entered with the same eight-to-ten-at-night interval given under Inu. The repetition is printed and is not removed as a duplicate.
Inuki means piercing through with an arrow or a projectile. Pilouro is the Portuguese projectile term, not another Japanese item.

runs.text: Erua aßi chamada agreſte de que fa-

lines.note: Inutade names a wild herb. The Portuguese says a sauce is made from it, beginning the verb fazem at the right edge.

runs.text: zem hũa ſalſa forte, & que requeima.

lines.note: Completes fazem and describes a strong, burning or pungent sauce. The culinary characterization belongs to the source and is preserved without botanical correction.
Inuzansho is described as a kind of wild Japanese pepper. The printed initial I is capital, and the circumflex in the headword contrasts with the caron in the following entry.
Insei and insho are alternative names for voices or vocal sounds, explained by koe. The alternative marker l and the printed caron in inxǒ are preserved.
Inshin is related to visiting or communicating and is glossed as a visit or a present. The capital I and the doubled zz in votozzure are visible; presente continues below.
Completes presente and gives inshin wo suru, glossed as visiting or sending a gift. The object of mandar continues on the next row.

After completing 'send a present', the entry gives inshin wo tsuuzuru, maintaining friendly communication. The upright S qualifies this example; Cõ- is the abbreviated beginning of the following Portuguese verb.

runs.text: municarſe com alguem por via de amizade cõ

lines.note: Completes comunicar-se and specifies friendly intercourse with someone. The final cõ introduces the means of that communication on the next row.
Messages or communications complete the explanation of inshin wo tsuuzuru. This short row closes the entry.

runs.text: Carta polla qual ſe viſita a alguem. Vt,

lines.note: Insho denotes a letter used to pay one's respects or make a visit in writing. The italic Vt introduces the acknowledgement formula below.

The Japanese formula expresses appreciation for the correspondent's letter. There is no separate pilcrow before Goinxo in the scan; the Portuguese starts the translated acknowledgement and retains the abbreviation q̃.

Completes the acknowledgement: the writer thanks the correspondent for the letter and is pleased with it. The scan restores viſitaſtes and agradeço from garbled OCR, and shows a real word space in com ella; the final S is upright.
